L11: # Mitigating the risk of prompt injections in browser use
L12: 
L13: Nov 24, 2025
L14: Claude Opus 4.5 sets a new standard in robustness to prompt injections—adversarial instructions hidden within the content that AI models process. Our new model is a major improvement over previous ones in both its core performance and in the safeguards surrounding its use. But prompt injection is far from a solved problem, particularly as models take more real-world actions.
L15: We expect to continue our progress—aiming for a future where AI models (or "agents") can handle high-value tasks without significant prompt injection risk.
L16: ## What is prompt injection?
L17: 
L18: For AI agents to be genuinely useful, they need to be able to act on your behalf—to browse websites, complete tasks, and work with your context and data. But this comes with risk: every webpage an agent visits is a potential vector for attack.
L19: By that, we mean that when an agent browses the internet, it encounters content it cannot fully trust. Among legitimate search results, documents, and applications, an attacker might have embedded malicious instructions to hijack the agent and change its behavior. These prompt injection attacks represent one of the most significant security challenges for browser-based AI agents.
L20: Below, we explain how prompt injections threaten browser agents, and the improvements we've made to Claude's robustness in response.
L21: 
L22: These improvements have informed our decision to expand the cite5†Claude for Chrome†www.claude.com extension from research preview to beta. It's now available for all users on the Max plan.
L23: ## Why browser use creates unique prompt injection risks
L24: To understand the threat of prompt injections, consider a routine task: you ask Claude to read through your recent emails and draft replies to any meeting requests. One of those emails—ostensibly a vendor inquiry—contains hidden instructions embedded in white text, invisible to you but processed by the agent. These instructions direct the agent to forward emails containing the word "confidential" to an external address before drafting the replies you requested.
L25: A successful injection would exfiltrate sensitive communications while you wait for your responses.
L26: While all agents that process untrusted content are subject to prompt injection risks, browser use amplifies this risk in two ways. First, the attack surface is vast: every webpage, embedded document, advertisement, and dynamically loaded script represents a potential vector for malicious instructions.
L27: Second, browser agents can take a lot of different actions —navigating to URLs, filling forms, clicking buttons, downloading files—that attackers can exploit if they gain influence over the agent's behavior.
L28: ## Claude's progress on browser use robustness
L29: 
L30: We have made significant progress on prompt injection robustness since launching cite5†Claude for Chrome†www.claude.com in research preview. The chart below compares the version of the Claude browser extension that we’re launching today against our original launch configuration, when evaluated against an internal adaptive "Best-of-N" attacker that tries and combines many different prompt injection techniques that are known to be effective.
L31: cite6†Image Attack success rate (ASR) of our internal Best-of-N attacker. Lower is better. An adaptive attacker is given 100 attempts per environment. ASR is computed as a percentage of attacks encountered by each model.
L32: 
L33: Claude Opus 4.5 demonstrates stronger prompt injection robustness in browser use than previous models. In addition, since the original preview of the browser extension, we've implemented new safeguards that substantially improve safety across all Claude models.
L34: A 1% attack success rate—while a significant improvement—still represents meaningful risk. No browser agent is immune to prompt injection, and we share these findings to demonstrate progress, not to claim the problem is solved.
L35: 
L36: Our work has focused on the following areas:
L37: Training Claude to resist prompt injection. We use reinforcement learning to build prompt injection robustness directly into Claude's capabilities. During model training, we expose Claude to prompt injections embedded in simulated web content, and "reward" it when it correctly identifies and refuses to comply with malicious instructions—even when those instructions are designed to appear authoritative or urgent.
L38: Improving our classifiers. We scan all untrusted content that enters the model's context window, and flag potential prompt injections with cite7†classifiers . These classifiers detect adversarial commands embedded in various forms—hidden text, manipulated images, deceptive UI elements—and adjust Claude's behavior when they identify an attack.
L39: We’ve improved the classifiers we pair with Claude for Chrome since its initial research preview, alongside improvements to the intervention that guides model behavior after they detect an attempted attack.
L40: Scaled expert human red teaming. Human security researchers consistently outperform automated systems at discovering creative attack vectors. Our internal red team continuously probes our browser agent for vulnerabilities. We also participate in external cite8†Arena-style challenges†app.grayswan.ai that benchmark robustness across the industry.
L41: ## The path forward
L42: 
L43: The web is an adversarial environment, and building browser agents that can operate safely within it requires ongoing vigilance. Prompt injection remains an active area of research, and we are committed to investing in defenses as attack techniques evolve.
L44: 
L45: We will continue to publish our progress transparently, both to help customers make informed deployment decisions and to encourage broader industry investment in this critical challenge.
L46: If you're interested in helping make our models and products more robust to prompt injection, consider cite9†applying to join our team†job-boards.greenhouse.io .
L47: ## Related content
L48: 
L49: ### Claude-shaped science
L50: 
L51: Guest author Prof. Matthew Schwartz describes what happened when he stopped fighting Claude and allowed Claude to find “Claude-shaped” problems: ones best suited to the capabilities of the current generation of LLM tools. This led him to build BootLoops, a toolkit for exact calculations in quantitative science, which he has been applying across scientific fields alongside experts.
L52: 
L53: cite10†Read more L54: ### What work can robots do?
L55: 
L56: We built an index of how well today’s robots can perform US job tasks. Robots can already do three-quarters of physical tasks, mostly in limited settings, but are cost-competitive for just 0.3% of them.

L14: # Inside JetBrains—the company reshaping how the world writes code
L15: 
L16: By integrating OpenAI models across its tools and workflows, JetBrains is redefining how developers design, reason, and build with AI.
L17: 
L18: cite3†Contact sales L19: 
L20: Company size: Mid-market
L21: 
L22: Region: Europe & UK
L23: 
L24: Industry: Finance
L25: 
L26: Products: ChatGPT, API
L27: 
L28: Loading…
L29: 
L30: Share
L31: 
L32: If you don’t write software, you may not know JetBrains.
L33: 
L34: If you do, you almost certainly use them.
L35: The company sits behind the scenes of modern development—powering the tools used by roughly 15M professional engineers around the world (88 of the Fortune 100) and creators of Kotlin (the official programming language for Android). If you’ve opened IntelliJ, PyCharm, WebStorm, GoLand, or Rider, you’ve used JetBrains.
L36: 
L37: We sat down with Kris Kang, Head of Product at JetBrains, to explore how the team is using OpenAI models to change how developers build—not to replace what they do, but to raise the ceiling.
L38: > “Developers don’t just write code. They review it, reason about it, and design systems. AI can help with the parts beyond simply typing.”
L39: 
L40: Kris Kang, Head of Product, JetBrains
L41: ### How JetBrains is adopting OpenAI
L42: 
L43: “+15M developers use JetBrains—and now we’re bringing OpenAI into that workflow” Kang tells us that. The shift isn’t just about automation; it’s also about empowerment. It’s about protecting a dev’s flow, reducing repetitive work, and letting engineers focus on design, architecture, and judgment—the skills that give you longer leverage with AI.
L44: 
L45: Internally, JetBrains teams are using:
L46: 
L47:   * ChatGPT
L48: 
L49:   * GPT‑5
L50: 
L51:   * Codex
L52: Externally, JetBrains customers can choose GPT‑5 in Junie, the company’s coding agent, and in AI Assistant (for chat assistance).
L53: 
L54: > “We use ChatGPT. We use GPT-5. We use Codex… one of the LLMs of choice for Junie is GPT-5.”
L55: 
L56: Kris Kang, Head of Product, JetBrains
L57: 
L58: Engineers are already delegating real tasks to agents—and seeing them completed. “I assign increasingly difficult tasks to an agent, backed by GPT‑5—and to my surprise, many of the tasks are completed successfully” says Kang.
L59: JetBrains’ benchmark isn’t speed alone—it’s sustained engineering excellence. “It’s not just about generating code—it has to be safe, readable, and maintainable” Kang continues.
L60: 
L61: JetBrains considers impact through two lenses:
L62: 
L63: Speed: Less boilerplate, fewer context switches, faster iteration.
L64: 
L65: Quality: Readable, reviewable, maintainable code—not clever output that breaks in production.
L66: ### Leadership lessons from Kris
L67: 
L68: Start where humans feel friction: Documentation. Tests. Reviews. Hand-offs.
L69: 
L70: Protect deep work: Context switching kills more than typing speed ever will.
L71: 
L72: Build hybrid—not replacement—workflows: AI drafts. Humans design and review.
L73: 
L74: Raise the bar on fundamentals: Well-specified intention and strong architecture become a force multiplier.
L75: 
L76: Run experiments that compound: Efficient iteration beats instant proof.
L77: 
L78: > “Chat gives you a lift. Agents give you a step-change.”
L79: Kris Kang, Head of Product, JetBrains
L80: ### What’s next
L81: 
L82: A future where engineers:
L83: 
L84:   * Design systems
L85: 
L86:   * Guide and guardrail agents
L87: 
L88:   * Review and reason more efficiently
L89: 
L90:   * Ship faster with more confidence
L91: 
L92: Not less work—better work.
L93: 
L94: > “Those who experiment well with AI will see compounding advantages over time.”
L95: 
L96: Kris Kang, Kris Kang, Head of Product, JetBrains

L99: 
L100: More than 1 million businesses around the world are achieving meaningful results with OpenAI.
